name: Maya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a five-person agency above a travel agent on the high street. We do a lot of print: restaurant menus, wedding invitations, posters for the theatre club, the odd logo. My day is mostly fiddling with layouts in InDesign, then running proofs to the print shop round the corner so the client can feel the paper.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy wedding stuff, it's fussy but people cry when they see it, in a good way. The hard part is I'm still slow and my boss Yusuf has to fix my kerning, which is the spacing between letters. And money's tight: Sam, my partner, is a shift supervisor at the parcel warehouse, and between us we've got about three weeks' worth saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it was always a bit overblown. I use a tool now and then to cut people out of photos, and it's handy, that's all. I'd say that to Yusuf over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means not much changes for me, which is good and bad. Good because my job's about as safe as it was. Bad because it wasn't that safe, and we still can't save properly with the rent where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask Yusuf for more time on the wedding work, because I'm better at it. I'd pick up a couple of private wedding stationery jobs on weekends. We'd try to save a bit more for a car, ours is dying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tired of thinking about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it wasn't that safe. What makes it shaky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restaurants are struggling round here. Two restaurants on the high street closed since summer, and every closed restaurant is a menu our agency never prints again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the small bit of automation touch in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The photo cut-outs and the resizing for social media. That's maybe an hour a day for me. I'd just fill that with more layout work, I think, if Yusuf has it.

say: I'd say AI was **overblown**, and I'm **not surprised**.
I'd say I use it for **photo cut-outs**, and that's handy, nothing more.
think: My job is about **as safe as before**, which isn't very safe.
do: Ask Yusuf for more time on **wedding work**.
Take a couple of **weekend stationery** jobs privately.
S0.quote: Two restaurants on the high street closed since summer, and every closed restaurant is a menu our agency never prints again.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **local business closures**, not AI.
The automated hour per day is easily **absorbed** in this world.
She sees **wedding stationery** as her strength.

steps.text: Ask Yusuf (her boss) to give her more wedding jobs
Take two private wedding stationery jobs on weekends
Save toward replacing the dying car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but kindly. I'd tell friends it's like when everyone had to learn computers. I'd also say the government should help with training costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency hires nobody new and maybe lets one of us go. I'm the slowest, so that's me. And Sam's warehouse already has sorting robots on one line, so it's both of us in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, every day, once Yusuf shows me which ones he trusts. I'd grow the wedding side, because couples still want a person. I'd ask Sam to look at the warehouse's maintenance training, someone has to fix the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the 'both of us' part that gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you. How would that look at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my agency lets me go and the parcel warehouse cuts Sam (her partner), we'd have about three weeks before the rent goes unpaid. We'd stop talking about a deposit and start talking about what we can cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for Yusuf to pick the tools. Why not pick them yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've wasted money on courses before. If Yusuf uses something every day, I know it works. I'm not first in the queue, but I'm not last either.

say: I'd say **adapt kindly**, like when everyone had to learn computers.
I'd say the government should help pay **training costs**.
think: The agency likely **cuts one person**, and I'm the slowest.
Sam's warehouse has **sorting robots**, so both our jobs are exposed.
do: Use the **AI tools daily** once Yusuf picks trusted ones.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly about **both of us** being at risk.
S1.quote: If my agency lets me go and the parcel warehouse cuts Sam (her partner), we'd have about three weeks before the rent goes unpaid.
fieldNote: She thinks about the **household**, not just her own job.
She waits for **proof from her boss** before adopting tools.
**Robot maintenance** is her idea for her partner.

steps.text: Use the AI layout tools Yusuf picks every working day
Advertise wedding stationery to local venues
Ask Sam to apply for robot maintenance training at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and governments need to step in with money for people. I'd share news stories, I wouldn't march. I'd be scared to say much at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my design job is gone in 2028, all of it is screen work. Sam's warehouse goes when the robots come, so around 2031. That gives us three years of his wage while I find something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight away: the gym, streaming, takeaways. I'd look for hands-on work, maybe at the print shop round the corner, running the machines and trimming. We'd stop paying into the car fund and just keep the old one going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums would you be doing at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sam's wage minus the rent, minus food, minus the car, and whatever is left is what we live on until 2031. Then I'd do them again, hoping for a different answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, a little, she's got a spare room. I'd hate it but we'd do it before we'd get into debt.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and governments must give people **money**.
I'd **share news stories** but keep quiet at work.
think: Sam's wage lasts until **robots in 2031**, giving us three years.
do: **Cut** the gym, streaming and takeaways at once.
Ask the **print shop** about running machines and trimming.
Stop the **car fund** and keep the old car.
S2.quote: My partner Sam's wage minus the rent, minus food, minus the car, and whatever is left is what we live on until 2031.
fieldNote: She treats her partner's **hands-on job** as the household's bridge.
Her own move is to **print production**, also hands-on.
Her mother's **spare room** is the last resort.

steps.text: Cancel the gym, streaming and takeaways straight away
Ask the print shop round the corner for machine work
Move into her mother's spare room if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's be sensible and plan. I'd say it at work too, Yusuf would agree. I'd want the government to fund courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is enough to switch properly. I think my design job thins out around 2029, so I'd want something else ready by then. Sam's warehouse would last to 2034, which gives us breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools at work to stay useful while it lasts. I'd do a part-time course in print finishing or signage next year. We'd save harder for two years, then look at whether to move somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can plan. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe back near my mum, rents are lower out there. There are no design jobs near my mum's village, but by 2031 there won't be design jobs anywhere, so that stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's a designer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for the fast version to scare you. Do one course this year, any course, and keep your hands busy too.

say: I'd say we've got time, so be **sensible and plan** ahead.
I'd want the **government to fund** courses for people in jobs like mine.
think: My screen-based design job **thins out** around 2029.
Sam's hands-on warehouse job lasts to **2034**, giving us breathing room.
do: Use **AI tools** at work to stay useful while the job lasts.
Take a **part-time course** in print finishing next year.
Save for two years, then think about **moving somewhere cheaper**.
S3.quote: There are no design jobs near my mum's village, but by 2031 there won't be design jobs anywhere, so that stops mattering.
fieldNote: She's **pragmatic**: plan, save, train, then decide.
Her partner's **later robot date** gives the household slack.
Moving home becomes **easier to accept** once design jobs vanish everywhere.

steps.text: Use AI layout tools at work every day
Take a part-time print finishing course next year
Save harder with Sam for two years
Look at renting near her mother's village after two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people are sensible. I'd tell my friends to do one thing a year to prepare. I don't think it's the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd have time to get good at design first and then move into something else. I'd be 37 in 2036. Sam and I could buy somewhere small and pay it down before robots reach the warehouse in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the agency and use the AI tools as Yusuf adopts them. In three or four years I'd look at moving into print production or teaching evening classes. We'd save for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Like any big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound more relaxed. Is there anything still nagging?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Junior designers like me still get squeezed in the first few years, long before 2036, so I'd still be the one most likely to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd have kids a bit sooner, while we both still have steady wages. It sounds odd, but that's how I'd think about it.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if people are sensible.
I'd tell friends to do **one thing a year** to prepare.
think: I'd have time to **get good** first, then move on.
Sam and I could **buy and pay down** a home before 2039.
do: Stay at the agency, using **AI tools** as Yusuf adopts them.
Look at **print production** or teaching in three or four years.
feel: **Uneasy** in a normal way, like any big change.
S4.quote: Junior designers like me still get squeezed in the first few years, long before 2036, so I'd still be the one most likely to go.
fieldNote: She is **relaxed** in tone, but still expects her **junior role** squeezed.
She'd bring **children forward** while wages are steady.
Ten years makes **buying a home** feel possible.

steps.text: Use the AI tools Yusuf adopts at the agency
Move into print production or teaching within four years
Save for a deposit on a small home with Sam
Plan to have children sooner while both wages are steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job and then Sam's three years later, with no time to plan. What would help is cheap or free courses for hands-on work, and some kind of payment while you're between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people will still want things made by a person. Couples still want a real person to design their wedding invitations, and I'm betting a bit of my future on that.

headlineQuote: Couples still want a real person to design their wedding invitations, and I'm betting a bit of my future on that.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old junior** designer at a print-heavy agency on the high street.
She uses AI now and then, waits for proof, and loves **wedding stationery**.
Her partner Sam supervises shifts at a **parcel warehouse**, so she thinks as a household.
She's **pragmatic**: plan, save, train, and accept moving home if needed.
She's **alarmed** by fast AGI and steadier when there are years to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking her job and then Sam's three years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Free courses** for hands-on work and **payment** between jobs.
